deep.reconstruction:
The page continues Gauss's table of decimal periods of 1/p for primes p, working downward through the primes between 500 and 1000. The previous page has 607 … 577; this page has 571, 569, 563, 557, 547, 541, 523, 521; the next page has 509 … 487.

The primes skipped between 500 and 571 are 509 (next page) and 503, 499 and 491 (next page too, below 500). Gauss also leaves out every prime whose period length is p−1 divided by an even number larger than 2: 593, 599, 601 and 607 are listed on the previous page, but 587 and 577 are listed while e.g. 613 and 617 are on other folios. Every prime between 521 and 571 does appear here.

For each p, Gauss writes the repetend of 1/p = 0.00d3 d4 d5 … in groups of 10 digits. He omits the two leading zeros, since 1/p < 1/100 for p > 100. He continues until the expansion visibly repeats and underlines the start of the repetition as a check.

In modern terms each entry gives the digits of N_p = (10^L − 1)/p, where L = ord_p(10). With the first two digits (00) dropped, the written string has L digits before the restart: L−2 digits of the period, then 00, then the period again.

Counting digits (the counts are mine):
- 571: 57 blocks = 570 digits, the last block ending in 00, then 1751313485 again. L = 570 = p−1, so 10 is a primitive root.
- 569: 28 blocks + '71', '00', then 175746… L = 284 = (p−1)/2.
- 563: 28 blocks + '0', then 177619893… The written run ends '…30' + '0'. L = 281 = (p−1)/2.
- 557: 28 blocks, of which the final '0017' (underlined) is the restart. L = 278 = (p−1)/2.
- 547: 9 blocks + '0', then 182815356… L = 91 = (p−1)/6.
- 541: 54 blocks = 540 digits, then 1848428835 underlined. L = 540 = p−1.
- 523: 26 blocks + '0', then 191204588… L = 261 = (p−1)/2.
- 521: 5 blocks + '00', then 19193857… L = 52 = (p−1)/10.

The digits are presumably produced by long division (repeated remainder 10r mod p). One could also use the multiplicative shortcuts Gauss describes in Disquisitiones art. 312–318: the digits of k/p are a cyclic shift of those of 1/p, located by the index of k. The page itself shows only results.

My own consistency checks:
- Quadratic character. 10 is a quadratic residue mod p iff (2/p)(5/p) = 1. That holds for 569, 563, 557, 547, 523 and 521, which all have L | (p−1)/2. It fails for 571 and 541, which are the full-period primes. All entries agree.
- Last digits. The period N_p must satisfy p·N_p ≡ −1 (mod 10^k). The final digits before the '00' agree with this:
  - 571 · …69 ≡ 99 (mod 100)
  - 547 · …17 ≡ 99
  - 521 · …19 ≡ 99

The red pencil strokes crossing the page are a later archival or 'done' cancellation mark, not mathematics. The pencil marks 'Math. 17', '441' and '(7)' are archival foliation.
errors: No arithmetic errors detected in the spot checks: leading digits of each 1/p, period lengths consistent with quadratic-residue character, and terminal digits satisfying p*N ≡ -1 mod 100. A full digit-by-digit verification needs a computer.

Several digits are overwritten or corrected in the manuscript, which suggests self-correction during computation. Examples are the 4th block of row 6 for 571 (7355516637), the 4th block of the last row for 571 (2609457092), and the 2nd block of row 2 for 523 (8680688336).

results.modern_name: Decimal expansion / repetend of 1/p; multiplicative order of 10 mod p (ord_p(10))
results.usually_credited_to: Tables of reciprocal periods: J. H. Lambert, Burckhardt, Gauss (Disquisitiones art. 312–318 and the table published in Werke II), later Reuschle, Shanks, Cunningham

results.what: The 10-digit grouping, the omission of the leading zeros and the underlining of the restart as a check give a table format for converting fractions with prime denominator into decimals.
results.modern_name: Table for converting common fractions to decimals (Gauss's 'Tafel zur Verwandlung gemeiner Brüche in Decimalbrüche')
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (published posthumously in Werke Bd. II)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a working sheet of Gauss's well-known table of decimal periods of 1/p for primes below 1000. The table is described in the Disquisitiones (art. 316–317) and printed in Werke II. The content is routine computation already attributed to him.

start and end of the 1/571 period as written
the complete 1/521 period matches the manuscript
the complete 1/547 period matches the manuscript

transcription_corrections: 'Math. 17' and '441' are pencil archival annotations; '(7)' is the circled folio number. None of these is mathematical content.
For 557, the final '0017' of the last block is underlined in the manuscript to mark the restart of the period. It is not part of the new period data.
